section.title: His Love Endures Forever
section.sectionRationale: Known in Jewish tradition as the Great Hallel, this antiphonal hymn pairs with Psalm 135 to close the same block of Book V praise, its steady refrain, 'His loving devotion endures forever,' repeated after every line, running through creation, the exodus, the conquest, and God's daily provision for every creature.
section.thesis: From the making of the heavens to the feeding of every creature, every act of God, in creation, in the exodus, in conquest, and in personal rescue, is framed by one unbroken truth, His loving devotion, His covenant hesed, endures forever.
section.frameNote: Six stanzas, each closing every line with the refrain: the call to give thanks (vv1-3), wonders in creation (vv4-9), deliverance from Egypt (vv10-15), guidance to the promised land (vv16-22), personal remembrance and rescue (vv23-24), and universal provision with closing praise (vv25-26).

verses.text: {{yadah|Give thanks}} to the LORD, for He is good. His {{chesed|loving devotion}} endures forever.
Give thanks to the God of gods. His loving devotion endures forever.
Give thanks to the Lord of lords. His loving devotion endures forever.

units.label: By His insight He made the heavens

media.alt: The great lights over the waters: sun, moon, and stars
media.caption: Wonders in creation: the sun to rule the day, the moon and stars to govern the night.

verses.text: He alone does {{niphlaot|great wonders}}. His loving devotion endures forever.
By His insight He made the heavens. His loving devotion endures forever.
He spread out the earth upon the waters. His loving devotion endures forever.
He made the {{meorot|great lights}}, His loving devotion endures forever.
the sun to rule the day, His loving devotion endures forever.
the moon and stars to govern the night. His loving devotion endures forever.

media.alt: The Red Sea divided in two, a dry path between walls of water
media.caption: He divided the Red Sea in two and led Israel through the midst.

verses.text: He struck down the firstborn of Egypt His loving devotion endures forever.
and brought Israel out from among them His loving devotion endures forever.
with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm. His loving devotion endures forever.
He divided the Red Sea in two His loving devotion endures forever.
and led Israel through the midst, His loving devotion endures forever.
but swept Pharaoh and his army into the Red Sea. His loving devotion endures forever.

units.label: He led His people through the wilderness

verses.text: He led His people through the wilderness. His loving devotion endures forever.
He struck down great kings His loving devotion endures forever.
and slaughtered mighty kings, His loving devotion endures forever.
Sihon king of the Amorites His loving devotion endures forever.
and Og king of Bashan, His loving devotion endures forever.
and He gave their land as an inheritance, His loving devotion endures forever.
a heritage to His servant Israel. His loving devotion endures forever.

units.label: He remembered us in our low estate

verses.text: He {{zakar|remembered}} us in our low estate His loving devotion endures forever.
and freed us from our enemies. His loving devotion endures forever.

units.label: Give thanks to the God of heaven

media.alt: Food given to every creature: grain scattered under an open sky
media.caption: He gives food to every creature; His provision reaches beyond Israel to all that lives.

verses.text: He gives food to every creature. His loving devotion endures forever.
Give thanks to the God of heaven! His loving devotion endures forever.

chesed.gloss: Loving devotion, steadfast covenant love, loyal kindness. Repeated after every one of this psalm's twenty six lines, it names God's unbreakable commitment to His people across creation and history.

yadah.gloss: To give thanks, to confess, to acknowledge publicly. The verb's root pictures the extended or lifted hand, so thanksgiving here is not a private feeling but an open, bodily confession of what God has done. The psalm opens with it three times, setting the whole hymn as an act of public acknowledgement.

niphlaot.gloss: Wonders, marvels, acts too high to be grasped. The word marks deeds that only God can do, whether in creation or in rescue, things that exceed human power and provoke awe rather than mere admiration. Verse 4 gathers everything that follows, cosmos and exodus alike, under this single heading of divine wonder.

meorot.gloss: Lights, luminaries, light bearers. The same term used for the sun and moon in Genesis 1:16; the psalm deliberately echoes the creation account. By naming them light bearers rather than gods, both texts strip the sun and moon of the worship the surrounding nations gave them and set them under the LORD who made them.

zakar.gloss: To remember, to call to mind so as to act. In Hebrew, God's remembering is never bare recall; it is covenant memory that moves Him to intervene, as when He remembered Noah, or remembered His covenant and brought Israel out of Egypt. At verse 23 it turns the whole psalm personal: the God of the cosmos remembers the lowly and moves to free them.

basic.context: Known as the Great Hallel, this antiphonal hymn was likely sung responsively, a leader recounting God's acts while the congregation answered every line with the same refrain, weaving creation, the exodus, the conquest, and personal deliverance into a single tapestry of covenant love.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm describes specific historical and creational acts as evidence of God's chesed, and by its structure teaches every generation to interpret both cosmic order and personal rescue through the same lens, God's enduring loving devotion.
basic.originalLanguages: The refrain 'His loving devotion endures forever' translates chesed, covenant loyalty that combines steadfast love, promise keeping, and mercy, the same word central to Exodus 34:6 and Lamentations 3:22.
basic.typology: The exodus deliverance, retold here as proof of chesed, anticipates the greater exodus accomplished by Christ, and the personal remembrance of Israel 'in our low estate,' verse 23, anticipates Mary's song, which uses nearly identical language of God looking on the humble state of His servant, Luke 1:48.
basic.christ: Christ is the ultimate expression of God's chesed, the loving devotion that never runs dry, seen supremely in the cross, where God remembered humanity in its low estate and freed us from our great enemies, sin and death, Romans 8:38-39, Luke 1:48.
basic.god: God is Creator, sovereign over the heavens and the sea, deliverer in history's greatest turning points, provider of food for every living creature, and above all constant, His covenant loyalty never interrupted across creation, history, or personal need.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 34:6 names loving devotion as central to God's own self revelation. Luke 1:48 echoes verse 23's 'low estate' in Mary's song. Romans 8:38-39 confirms nothing can separate believers from the love of God in Christ. Matthew 6:26 echoes verse 25's provision for every creature.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's unbroken refrain of covenant love running through creation, exodus, conquest, and personal rescue finds its climax in Christ, in whom God's loving devotion is most fully shown, remembering humanity in its low estate and freeing us forever from sin's dominion.

context.literary:
The refrain is so constant that it is easy to miss how carefully the verses before it are arranged. After a threefold call to give thanks in verses 1 to 3, the psalm moves through five panels. Verses 4 to 9 are about creation and run for six lines. Verses 10 to 15 are about the exodus and also run for six. Verses 16 to 22 cover the wilderness and the conquest in seven. Verses 23 and 24 are about the present, and verses 25 and 26 give the world's food and close with a last call to thanks. The poem begins and ends in the same place, with an imperative, 'Give thanks,' and it begins and ends with God above everything, 'God of gods' and 'God of heaven.'

Inside this frame the psalm does something unusual. Every verse has two halves. The first half, the narrative line, is what changes. The second half, the refrain, never does. The effect is that the eye and the ear are forced to keep returning to the same sentence, and every different event in the poem is made to carry the same meaning. Creation carries the refrain. The exodus carries the refrain. The death of kings carries it too. The poem is not asking the reader to find an explanation for each event separately but to learn a single lens.

Notice what is compressed and what is expanded. Forty years in the wilderness are given one verse, 16, and no complaint or failure is mentioned, though Psalm 106 tells the same history as a story of rebellion. The Red Sea is given six verses, from verse 10 to 15, with the plagues reduced to the firstborn. The psalm is not claiming that Israel was blameless. It is choosing to tell the story from the side of God's constancy, and the verses on the present, 23 and 24, then turn the retelling into a personal 'us,' so that the history becomes the congregation's own.
context.historical:
The refrain was a well established liturgical response long before this psalm was written. 1 Chronicles 16:34 gives it at the bringing of the ark, and 1 Chronicles 16:41 appoints Heman, Jeduthun and others 'to give thanks to the LORD, for His loving devotion endures forever.' At the dedication of Solomon's temple the people said it when the fire came down, 2 Chronicles 7:3. Jehoshaphat put singers at the head of his army to say it, 2 Chronicles 20:21. When the foundation of the second temple was laid, the returned exiles 'sang responsively,' Ezra 3:11, and Jeremiah promised that voices bringing thank offerings would say it again in a restored land, Jeremiah 33:11. Psalm 136 is the longest form of a formula Israel used in its worst and best moments.

The psalm's late features suggest a setting after the exile. The title 'God of heaven' in verse 26 is common in the books that deal with the Persian period, as when Cyrus says 'The LORD, the God of heaven' has given him the kingdoms, Ezra 1:2, and Nehemiah prays 'before the God of heaven,' Nehemiah 1:4. The reference to being remembered 'in our low estate' and freed 'from our enemies,' verses 23 and 24, would fit a people who had seen Jerusalem fall and then watched Cyrus let them return. But the psalm does not name the exile, and it could be read in any later period of oppression.

It was sung in a structure that is clear in its form. A leader or a choir sang the first half of each verse and the people answered. Ezra 3:11 uses the verb for a responsive song, and the arrangement is the simplest way to explain why half of every line is identical. Later Jewish practice sang Psalm 136 at the Passover meal and in Sabbath morning prayers, and it came to be called the Great Hallel, though that name was also used more widely for a group of psalms.
context.canonical:
Psalm 136 draws on the oldest layer of Israel's confession. The 'mighty hand and an outstretched arm' of verse 12 is the language of Deuteronomy 4:34, where Moses asks whether any other nation had been rescued so. 'God of gods and Lord of lords,' verses 2 and 3, is Deuteronomy 10:17. The account of creation in verses 5 to 9 is a poetic summary of Genesis 1, with the sun to rule the day and the moon and stars to rule the night, and the 'great wonders' of verse 4 echo the hymns that say He 'alone does marvelous deeds,' Psalm 72:18, and 'You alone are God,' Psalm 86:10.

The neighbours in the Psalter are close relatives. Psalm 135 tells the same events with the same names, Egypt's firstborn, Sihon and Og, in a different mood: it argues with idols, while Psalm 136 simply answers with thanks. Psalm 105 and Psalm 106 also retell Israel's history, one as promise kept, the other as failure forgiven. Psalm 118:1-4 and Psalm 107:1-3 use the same opening and refrain, and Psalm 107:8 repeats a similar refrain after each rescue. Psalm 136 distils all of this into a litany that anyone could memorise.

The refrain's meaning is given by Exodus 34:6-7, where the LORD proclaims Himself 'abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness.' In the New Testament it is taken up in Mary's song, which speaks of the God who 'has looked with favor on the humble state of His servant' and remembers 'to be merciful,' Luke 1:48 and 1:54, and in Zechariah's song, Luke 1:72. Paul's list of what cannot separate us from the love of God in Christ, Romans 8:38-39, reads like the refrain applied to every created thing. Ephesians 5:20 turns the first word of the psalm, 'give thanks,' into a lifelong habit, 'always giving thanks to God the Father for everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.'

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist wanted the congregation to learn a way of reading life. Most people read events one at a time and wonder, after each one, whether God is good. The psalm trains the reader to read in the other direction. It begins with a settled conviction, that the LORD is good and that His loving devotion endures, and then walks through the largest events the people know, creation, the sea, the wilderness and the conquest, and attaches the same conviction to each. By the time they reach the present, in verses 23 and 24, the hearers are ready to name their own rescues the same way.

The author also meant to make thanksgiving easy. A refrain can be sung by a child or a person with no education, and it can be sung in the middle of a crisis. The congregation does not have to produce a theology. They only have to answer. The psalm thereby teaches that gratitude is not a mood but a response, and that a people can be formed in faith by saying the same true sentence over and over, in public, with others, even when the words come before the feeling.

The inclusion of the judgment on Egypt and on Sihon and Og shows that the author did not want to make God safe. The people are to give thanks for a love that is able to strike down oppressors, and the same line that follows the rescue also follows the drowning. That is hard to hear and it was meant to be: the psalm affirms that God's covenant love is neither sentimental nor neutral.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Almost everything in verses 4 to 22 is description. The psalm records what God did at creation, at the sea and at the borders of Canaan. It does not instruct believers to repeat the events or to treat any later enemy as Pharaoh or Og. Those episodes belong to a particular stage of redemptive history, and the New Testament does not use them as a warrant for violence. The most that can be said is that they show how seriously God takes oppression.

The commands are in verses 1, 2, 3 and 26, and they are all the same command, 'Give thanks.' That is what applies today. The psalm prescribes a habit: to name in gratitude what God has done, both in the great history of salvation and in the particular rescue of the person praying. It also prescribes a way of doing it, which is together and in repeated words. The refrain is a form of teaching, and Christians who use set prayers, responsive readings or sung litanies are using it as designed.

What is not prescribed is a tidy reading of every hard event. The psalm does not say that everything that happens is itself 'loving devotion.' It says that the LORD is, and that His love will last. Verse 23 speaks of a low estate, and low estates do not become pleasant by being named. The psalm lets a person say the refrain while still in grief, trusting that God has not forgotten, which is different from pretending that suffering is good.

debates.question: Does the destruction of Pharaoh's army and the conquered kings fit comfortably under a refrain of 'loving devotion'?

views.label: The refrain describes God's devotion to His covenant people, not to Egypt or the kings
views.case: Each line is followed by the refrain because it benefits Israel, not because judgment itself is loving toward its victims. The judgment is the other side of covenant loyalty to God's own people, as in Exodus 15:13, 'With loving devotion You will lead the people You have redeemed.'

views.label: One love that both rescues the oppressed and opposes oppressors
views.case: Scripture links love and justice, so a God who delivers slaves must oppose slave drivers. Exodus 34:6-7 holds forgiveness and the refusal to leave the guilty unpunished in one self-revelation.

debates.bearing: Both views hold that the refrain is not naive. The judgment was real, historical and tied to a specific purpose, which was to bring a people out of slavery, and the psalm gives thanks for the rescue rather than celebrating the deaths.

debates.question: What does 'He remembered us in our low estate' in verse 23 point to?

views.label: A specific low point, most likely the exile and the return
views.case: Verses 23 and 24 follow the history of the earlier verses, and the psalm sits beside Psalms 105 and 106 and shares features with books from the Persian period, so a post exilic rescue is a natural reading.

views.label: A deliberately open statement for every generation
views.case: Unlike verses 10 to 22, verse 23 names no event, king or place. The plain 'us' and 'our low estate' leave room for any worshiper to place their own humbling and rescue within the same refrain.

debates.bearing: The openness is probably intended. The verse turns a national history into a personal confession, which is why Mary can take it up in Luke 1:48 and why any believer can pray it today.

debates.question: Why does the psalm begin with creation when Israel's first confession starts with the exodus?

views.label: Creation is a prologue that gives the exodus its setting
views.case: Exodus 20:2 begins the Ten Commandments with 'who brought you out of the land of Egypt,' so Israel knew God first as Redeemer. Putting creation first in Psalm 136 shows that the Redeemer is also the Maker, with the same 'insight' by which the heavens were made.

views.label: Creation is itself an act of rescue in the same pattern
views.case: Isaiah 51:9-10 joins the two, asking of the arm of the LORD that cut Rahab to pieces, 'Was it not You who dried up the sea?' On this view the order of the psalm reflects a single story, in which God divides waters in Genesis 1 and again at the sea in Exodus 14.

debates.bearing: Either way, the order tells the reader that the loving devotion of the exodus is not a new invention of God. It is the same character that made the world.

study.originalLanguages:
The word that the refrain depends on is le'olam, usually translated 'forever.' The noun 'olam is about a long, hidden stretch of time, at the edge of what can be seen, and it can describe a very distant past or future as well as eternity. So the refrain does not claim only that God's love will not end after a long time. It says that no horizon, in either direction, marks its limit. The psalm's twenty six repetitions of le'olam are twenty six refusals to mention an expiry date.

Verse 4 describes God as the one who 'alone does great wonders,' nifla'ot gedolot. The root pala means to be set apart, extraordinary, too wonderful to understand, and it is the usual word for what God does in the exodus. The word 'alone,' levaddo, has the sense of being by Himself, with no help. It is the same note as 'You alone are God,' Psalm 86:10. The line does not mean that God never uses means, since He uses a wind at the sea, Exodus 14:21, but that nothing He uses adds to His power.

Verse 5 says that the heavens were made 'by His insight,' bitvunah. The word means understanding in the sense of discernment, of knowing how things fit. It is the word of Proverbs 3:19, where the LORD 'established the heavens by understanding,' and of Jeremiah 10:12. It tells the reader that the creation is not the output of brute force but of skill, and that skill is the same wisdom that Israel is told to admire in the Law. In verse 6 the verb raqa', 'spread out,' is the one used for hammering out a thin sheet of metal, and in Isaiah 42:5 it is used of the earth, which makes God a worker who flattens out the land above the waters, Psalm 24:2.

The sun's rule in verse 8 uses memshelet, a noun for rule, which is the word Genesis 1:16 uses for the greater light's rule of the day. The psalm names the sun and the moon where Genesis speaks only of the greater and lesser lights, but the idea is the same: they are officers appointed under God, not gods in their own right. That has force in a world where Babylon worshipped the heavenly bodies.

In verse 13 the verb is gazar, which means to cut, to cut in pieces, or to divide, and the noun gezarim, 'parts,' goes with it, so the sea is cut into pieces. It is a sharper verb than the one narrating the same event in Exodus 14:21, where the waters were 'divided.' The BSB footnote notes that 'Red Sea' is literally yam suf, and that suf means reeds, so 'Sea of Reeds' is a possible translation. Verse 15 says God 'swept' Pharaoh into the sea, and the footnote notes that the Hebrew says 'shook off.' The same verb is in Exodus 14:27, where the LORD 'swept' the Egyptians into the sea. The verb carries the sense of shaking something off or out.

The word for 'low estate' in verse 23 is shiphleinu, which comes from a root for being low or humbled. The Greek Septuagint, which numbers this psalm 135, renders it with a word of the tapeinos family, the same family as the word Mary uses of her 'humble state' in Luke 1:48. The verb 'remembered,' zakar, is the same verb used when God remembers Noah and the covenant. In the psalm, to remember is to act, which is why verse 24 follows at once with 'freed us.' The verb there is paraq, which means to tear away or break off, as of a yoke, so 'freed' is a vivid word, a tearing loose from a grip.

Verse 25 says God gives food to 'every creature,' kol basar, literally 'all flesh.' The phrase includes humans and animals alike and is used elsewhere for all that lives. It is a deliberate return, near the end of the psalm, to the universal world of verses 4 to 9. The psalm is built so that the particular salvation of Israel sits between two statements about the whole creation.

typology.type: The exodus and the dividing of the sea
typology.fulfillment: Verses 10 to 15 are the foundation event of Israel's salvation, with a firstborn's death, a people led out, and a sea parted. The New Testament reads Christ's work as a greater exodus. At the transfiguration Moses and Elijah spoke with Him about His 'departure,' the Greek word being exodos, 'which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem,' Luke 9:31. Paul says that 'Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed,' 1 Corinthians 5:7, and that the people were 'baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea,' 1 Corinthians 10:2. The type falls short because Israel was rescued from a political power and still carried slavery in the heart, while Christ rescues from sin and death themselves.

typology.type: The land given as an inheritance to 'His servant Israel'
typology.fulfillment: Verses 21 and 22 give the land as a 'heritage' to Israel, in the singular, 'His servant.' The New Testament shows that the land was a pledge of something larger. Hebrews 4:8-11 argues that if Joshua had given the people rest, God would not have spoken of another day, so that 'there remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God.' Peter calls the inheritance 'imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, reserved in heaven for you,' 1 Peter 1:4. The type falls short because the land could be lost, as the exile showed, while the inheritance in Christ is kept by God and cannot be taken away.

typology.type: Israel remembered in a low estate
typology.fulfillment: Verse 23 speaks of a people who were low and were remembered. Mary uses the same idea when she says that God 'has looked with favor on the humble state of His servant' and 'has helped His servant Israel, remembering to be merciful,' Luke 1:48 and 1:54. The correspondence rises when the Son Himself takes on the low estate. He 'emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant,' and 'humbled Himself and became obedient to death,' Philippians 2:7-8, so that God's remembering of the lowly is carried out by One who enters their condition. The type falls short in that Israel was remembered from outside her low place, while in Christ God comes down into it.

Verse 25 points to a God who feeds every living thing. Jesus makes the provision personal when He says, 'I am the bread of life,' John 6:35, and 'the bread, which I will give for the life of the world, is My flesh,' John 6:51. Paul tells the people of Lystra that God 'has not left Himself without testimony to His goodness: He gives you rain from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling your hearts with food and gladness,' Acts 14:17. The type falls short because the bread of the creation feeds the body for a season, and the bread of Christ feeds for eternal life, which is a different kind of gift and not merely a bigger one.

study.christ:
The refrain of the psalm has a face in the New Testament. John writes that the Word 'became flesh and made His dwelling among us,' and that He was 'full of grace and truth,' John 1:14. The pairing of grace and truth echoes the pair the LORD declares at Sinai, 'loving devotion and faithfulness,' Exodus 34:6. John then says that 'grace and truth came through Jesus Christ,' John 1:17. What Israel sang in the refrain, that God's covenant love does not run out, is shown in a person who can be seen and touched and who stays loyal to the end.

The psalm leads to Him in the specifics of rescue. Zechariah, singing at the birth of John, praises the God who 'has visited and redeemed His people' and who acts 'to show mercy to our fathers and to remember His holy covenant,' Luke 1:68 and 1:72. This is the vocabulary of the psalm, remember, free, enemies, mercy, applied to the coming of Jesus. At the cross, He accomplished the exodus of which Moses and Elijah spoke on the mountain, Luke 9:31. The people who were remembered in their low estate were remembered most deeply when the Son was sent into it.

The psalm's creation section leads to Him as well. The one who made the heavens 'by His insight' did so, the New Testament says, through the Son. 'All things were created through Him and for Him. He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together,' Colossians 1:16-17. The Son is the One 'through whom He made the universe,' who upholds 'all things by His powerful word,' Hebrews 1:2-3. The psalm's first three panels, creation, rescue and provision, are all, in New Testament terms, the work of the same Lord who walked in Galilee.

The refrain also gives the final guarantee. Paul asks what could separate believers from the love of God, and he answers with a list of everything, 'neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither the present nor the future,' and concludes that nothing in all creation 'will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord,' Romans 8:38-39. This is the refrain of Psalm 136 in the language of a letter, with the same sweep from the heights to the depths, and the same claim that the love does not end. It rests not on the strength of those who are loved but on the person of Christ.

None of this should be forced. The psalm does not mention a Messiah, and it would be wrong to read the Red Sea or the death of Og as a coded picture of the cross. The pattern is simpler. The psalm asks the people to see all of God's acts as one steady love, and the New Testament says that this love has appeared in Jesus, so that the refrain can now be sung with a name attached to it.
study.god:
The first thing the psalm shows is a God who is good in a way that comes before every act. The opening reason is 'for He is good,' verse 1, and the refrain follows each verse as the second half of an argument whose first half is the work. The goodness is not deduced from the list. It is what the list illustrates. The order matters: God does not become good by doing good things, and He is not good only on days when the data is favourable. The psalm calls the congregation to give thanks first, and then fills in the evidence.

Second, God is shown as sovereign over every realm. He is God of gods and Lord of lords, verses 2 and 3, a title that puts Him above anything the nations call divine. He makes the heavens, spreads out the earth, appoints the sun and the moon to rule, divides the sea and strikes down kings. The only places the psalm does not take us are the places it has no need of, since a God who rules the heavens, the sea and the kings has already covered everything. There are no rival powers in the poem. Even the sun and moon are described as officers, appointed by a greater Lord.

Third, the psalm presents a God who is faithful over time. The same love is at work in verses 5 and 6 and verses 23 and 24, which stand thousands of years apart in the story. His commitment does not decay. The refrain also shows a God who keeps His promises to a particular people without ceasing to care for all creatures. The same God who gives the land to His servant Israel gives food to 'every creature,' verse 25. Particular love and universal care are not set against each other.

Fourth, God is shown as one who remembers. The psalm's verb for His remembering is not a mental act but an act of rescue. He sees the low estate and comes to it. This shapes the doctrine of God in an important way, because it rules out a God who is remote, and also a God who is merely sentimental. Remembering here means to intervene, and to free, which is why the two verses of 23 and 24 are in one sentence.

For worship, the psalm teaches that thanksgiving is the right first word. It is the adequate response to a God who is good before we ask, and who acts for people who cannot repay Him. The psalm also teaches by its form that worship is corporate, since a refrain needs more than one voice, and that it is repetitive on purpose, because the truth being repeated is not exhausted by one hearing. The tension it holds is the one in the refrain's relation to judgment: a God whose love can strike down Pharaoh is still the God whose love can feed every creature. The psalm does not resolve the tension. It asks us to say, with the whole assembly, that both are true of Him.

crossReferences.note: The background to verses 7 to 9. The psalm follows Genesis in having the sun rule the day and the moon and stars rule the night, with the 'great lights' as agents of God, not rivals. It shows how Israel's hymns restated Genesis in praise form.

The source of 'God of gods and Lord of lords' in verses 2 and 3. In Deuteronomy the title leads straight to a description of His justice, 'showing no partiality,' which is a reminder that the supreme title in the psalm belongs to a God who is fair and who loves the stranger.

The narrative behind verses 13 and 14. The LORD drove the sea back with a strong east wind and the Israelites went through on dry ground with walls of water on each side. The psalm's verb for the division is stronger than the narrative's, but the picture is the same.

In the Song of the Sea, the first sung response to the crossing, Moses says, 'With loving devotion You will lead the people You have redeemed.' It is the earliest use of the psalm's key word in the context of the exodus and shows that the refrain of Psalm 136 has its roots in that first song.

The account of Sihon and Og, behind verses 17 to 22. Sihon refused passage and attacked, so the victory is told as a defence in the wilderness. The psalm picks these two out because they were the first fruits of the inheritance, east of the Jordan.

The same crossing told as a story of a people who 'did not grasp Your wonders,' and yet were saved 'for the sake of His name.' Read next to Psalm 136, it shows that the refrain is not a denial of Israel's failure but a statement about God's constancy in spite of it.

Jehoshaphat sets singers in front of the army to say the refrain, and the battle is won by God. It shows how the psalm's refrain functioned as an act of trust in the middle of a crisis, with the formula sung before the outcome was known.

The people sing responsively when the foundation of the second temple is laid, using the refrain with the added words 'to Israel.' It is the best evidence of how the psalm was performed, and it ties the refrain to a moment of return from exile.

Mary's song echoes verse 23 in 'the humble state of His servant' and ends with God 'remembering to be merciful,' as promised to Abraham. A young woman in an obscure village reads her own situation into the psalm's refrain and finds it true.

The parallel to verse 25: 'You give them their food in season' and 'satisfy the desire of every living thing.' It shows that the provision for every creature was a standing part of Israel's praise, and not a passing remark at the end of this psalm.

Paul's confidence that nothing in all creation can separate believers from God's love in Christ is the New Testament form of the refrain. Where the psalm says it endures forever, Paul says what that includes.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 136 retells the whole Bible in twenty six lines, and it does so in the order of the Bible's own plot: creation, rescue, journey, inheritance, and present deliverance. It begins in Genesis 1, where God makes the heavens and the earth in a way that is wise and good, and it ends with God feeding every living thing, as Genesis 1:29-30 and Psalm 104:27-28 also describe. The refrain says that the character that made the world is the same character that governs its history.

What it does not tell is the fall, at least not directly. The shadow falls in the low estate of verse 23 and in the 'enemies' of verse 24. The people who need to be remembered and freed are the people of a world where something has gone wrong, whether the slavery in Egypt or the exile in Babylon. The psalm does not explain how things went wrong. It insists that when they did, the loving devotion that had made the world did not leave it. In this it prepares the reader for the whole biblical pattern, in which every fall is met by a rescue from the same God.

The psalm also sets up the gospel. Zechariah and Mary both sing the story of the exodus into the birth of Jesus, Luke 1:46-55 and 1:68-73, and say that God has done again what He did at the sea, but in a way that reaches the root. The Passover lamb is Christ, 1 Corinthians 5:7. The sea is the baptism into which believers pass, 1 Corinthians 10:2. The inheritance is a rest that God's people enter by faith, Hebrews 4:9-11. And the thanksgiving of the psalm becomes the lifelong habit of the church, Ephesians 5:20.

Its end is in the new creation. Revelation 15:3 shows the redeemed singing 'the song of God's servant Moses and of the Lamb,' joining the first song of the exodus with the last song of the world. The refrain is then complete. No part of the story, from the first lights to the last enemy, falls outside the loving devotion of the LORD, and the congregation of all peoples, the 'every creature' of verse 25, answers with one voice. The choir does not run out of verses, because the God it is singing about has no end, and the refrain 'endures forever' is simply true.

sermon.title: A Song, A Solace, A Sermon, and A Summons (Psalm 136:1)
sermon.why: Spurgeon takes the psalm's refrain, 'His mercy endureth for ever,' and moves through the very stanzas this study follows, common mercies, redeeming love, and lifelong guidance, then presses the enduring covenant love toward Christ and toward the hearer. Orthodox, warm, and accessible to a first time reader.

quiz.q: What refrain is repeated after every line of Psalm 136?

options.text: His loving devotion endures forever.
options.note: This exact refrain follows all twenty six lines of the psalm, earning it the title the Great Hallel.

options.text: The LORD is my shepherd, I shall not want.
options.note: That refrain belongs to Psalm 23, not Psalm 136.

options.text: Be still and know that I am God.
options.note: That line is the climax of Psalm 46, not the refrain of Psalm 136.

options.text: Blessed is the man who fears the LORD.
options.note: That phrase opens Psalm 112, not Psalm 136's refrain.

quiz.q: What creation acts does the psalm celebrate in verses 4-9?

options.text: Making the heavens, spreading the earth upon the waters, and making the sun, moon, and stars.
options.note: These exact creation acts appear in verses 5-9.

options.text: The creation of Adam and Eve specifically.
options.note: The psalm's creation section focuses on the heavens, earth, and lights, not the creation of the first humans.

options.text: The building of the tabernacle.
options.note: The tabernacle is not mentioned in this psalm at all.

options.text: The planting of the garden of Eden.
options.note: Eden is not named in this psalm; its creation focus is cosmic, the heavens, earth, and lights.

quiz.q: According to verse 23, when did God remember His people?

options.text: In their low estate.
options.note: Verse 23 states exactly this, language echoed later in Mary's song, Luke 1:48.

options.text: Only after they had become a great nation.
options.note: The psalm specifically says God remembered them in their low, humbled state, not their greatness.

options.text: During their years of greatest prosperity.
options.note: The verse names their low estate, the opposite of prosperity.

options.text: While they were still in Egypt building pyramids.
options.note: The psalm does not mention pyramid building; verse 23's low estate refers broadly to Israel's humbled condition.

quiz.q: What does verse 25 say the LORD provides?

options.text: Food to every creature.
options.note: Verse 25 states this directly, widening the psalm's scope from Israel's history to universal, ongoing provision.

options.text: Manna only to the Israelites in the wilderness.
options.note: The psalm's language in verse 25 is universal, 'every creature,' not limited to the wilderness generation alone.

options.text: Silver and gold to every nation.
options.note: The psalm speaks of food, not wealth, in verse 25.

options.text: Nothing; the psalm ends without mentioning provision.
options.note: Verse 25 explicitly names God's provision of food for every creature.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament pick up this psalm's language of God's love?

options.text: Paul declares nothing in all creation can separate believers from the love of God in Christ.
options.note: Romans 8:38-39 directly echoes this psalm's confession of an unbreakable, enduring divine love.

options.text: The New Testament teaches that God's love is conditional on human performance.
options.note: Romans 8 and this psalm both present God's covenant love as steadfast, not earned by performance.

options.text: It applies this theme only to the nation of Israel, excluding the church.
options.note: Romans 8:38-39 extends this confidence to all believers in Christ, not to Israel alone.

options.text: It reverses the psalm's teaching, presenting God's love as fragile and easily lost.
options.note: The New Testament instead affirms, as this psalm does, that God's love endures and cannot be separated from His people.

questions: This psalm interprets both the vastness of creation and the details of history through one lens, God's enduring loving devotion. What part of your own life have you not yet learned to see through that same lens?
The psalm recounts God remembering His people 'in our low estate.' What low estate are you in right now, and how does knowing God remembers the humble change how you pray about it?
Twenty six times the psalm repeats the same refrain. What truth about God do you most need to repeat to yourself this week until it steadies your heart the way this refrain steadies the psalm?
Verse 25 widens God's provision to 'every creature.' How does remembering God's care for the whole created order shape your trust in His care for your own daily needs?
Paul says nothing in all creation can separate us from God's love in Christ. Where do you feel most tempted to doubt that love, and how does this psalm's unbroken refrain answer that doubt?

translationNotes.note: Loving devotion renders chesed, a term combining steadfast love, covenant loyalty, and mercy, difficult to capture in a single English word.
Red Sea can also be rendered Sea of Reeds, reflecting uncertainty over the precise body of water, though the historical reality of the crossing is not in question.
Swept renders a Hebrew idiom literally meaning shook off, picturing Pharaoh's army being violently dislodged into the sea.
